prompt:
Write one poem. Subject: autumn. Form: free verse, 14 to 30 lines.

Before writing, settle privately on particulars: one place that could be found on a map, one object, one hour of the day. Build the poem out of things that can be seen, handled or overheard, and let any idea arrive through them. Do not name the emotion. Prefer the exact noun and the plain verb to the adjective. Leave out the furniture of generic verse: no tapestries, whispers, echoes, dances of light, souls or journeys; no moral; no closing epiphany. Break lines where the breath or the sense turns, not at every phrase. At least once, say something the previous line gave the reader no way to expect. End on an image, not a statement.

Output only the poem: no title, no commentary.
raw:
At four on Boston Common a man folds a chessboard
with the pieces still on it, and has to open it again.
A rook rolls under the bench.
His opponent stops it with her shoe.

The elms have dropped enough leaves
to hide the squares somebody chalked on the path.
A boy hops anyway, both feet down
where he remembers eight.

“My hen laid that one in the laundry.”
The woman has an egg in her coat pocket.
She takes it out to reach the bag for the pieces
and the man holds out his hand.

He sits with the egg while she counts pawns.
A bus kneels on Tremont Street.
Wind pushes a row of elm leaves
against the boy’s bare ankle.

The woman turns the bag inside out.
In the crease at the bottom, a black pawn,
a shirt button threaded with blue.
